document.title: Forecasters who skip questions score better, and the best filter reads the probability
document.standfirst: In 410,451 forecasts from the Good Judgment Project, a filter that holds back forecasts by their stated probability cut the average error far more than one that reads the forecaster's own expertise rating. People who skip more questions also score better on their first answers, though a person who skips more in one year is not clearly better for it.
document.tier_reason: Large real data with working shuffle controls and a preregistration. Skips are inferred and causation is open, and a filter on stated probability lowers the Brier score partly by arithmetic. Merkle and colleagues (2017) is close prior work on selection.
document.rung_reason: A preregistration with pass-or-fail rules is on file, which this rung needs. The next rung needs a named rival reading beaten by a decisive observation, and none is on file.
document.objection: Inferred skips may be questions a forecaster never saw; matched strata may explain any difference in sign from Merkle and colleagues, whose sign we have not confirmed; a filter on stated probability rewards confidence by construction.
document.objection_source: the strongest objection recorded in our publication register
document.would_change: Replicate on another tournament where question exposure is visible; read Merkle and colleagues in full.

sections.title: What this means for a reader
paragraphs: When a forecaster, a panel or a software system has to choose which answers to withhold, the number it already states is a much better guide than how expert it says it is. In a large public forecasting tournament, a filter on the stated probability cut the error of kept forecasts about six times as much as a filter on self-rated expertise, and the self-rating added nothing a shuffled rating did not also add. People who answer selectively are better forecasters on average, so a habit of skipping marks a careful source. The data does not show that skipping a question makes the remaining answers better.

sections.title: Abstract
paragraphs: A source that may decline to answer needs a rule for which answers to hold back. We tested two candidate inputs for that rule on the public survey forecasts of the Good Judgment Project: the probability the forecaster stated, and the forecaster's own 1 to 5 rating of their expertise on that forecast. On 410,451 binary forecasts, filters were scored by the area under the risk-coverage curve, the mean Brier score of kept forecasts as coverage falls from 100 to 10 percent. {c1}A filter on the stated probability scored 0.171, a filter on the self-rating 0.259, and random order 0.277.{/c1} {c2}Adding the self-rating to the probability gained 0.0026 (95 percent interval 0.0007 to 0.0046), under the preregistered bar of 0.005, and a rating shuffled within each forecaster-year gained 0.0024 on average.{/c2} We also asked whether people who skip questions forecast better. {c3}On first forecasts only, skip rate correlated with better relative Brier score at rho +0.286 (+0.264 to +0.303) across 9,204 forecaster-years, and +0.195 (+0.174 to +0.212) when timing was matched as well.{/c3} {c4}Within the same person across consecutive years the correlation was +0.041 (-0.007 to +0.095) over 1,578 pairs, so no within-person benefit of skipping was shown.{/c4} {c5}Forecasts rated expertise 1 are pulled toward 50 percent by about the right amount: the best extremising factor was 0.92 (0.79 to 1.06).{/c5}

sections.title: Introduction and motivation
paragraphs: The Good Judgment Project ran from 2011 to 2015 as one of several research teams in a geopolitical forecasting tournament. Thousands of volunteers gave probabilities for world events, and the project tested training, teaming and tracking of top performers as ways to raise accuracy {cite:r2}. The survey forecasts, with each forecaster's self-rated expertise on each forecast for the first three years, are public.

Forecasters in the project chose which questions to answer. That choice is part of the data. Merkle, Steyvers, Mellers and Tetlock {cite:r3} asked whether good and poor forecasters choose questions differently, and whether those choices can sharpen estimates of a forecaster's ability beyond what a {g:proper-scoring-rule}proper scoring rule{/g} reads from the forecasts alone. A proper scoring rule, in decision theory, is a score that a forecaster does best on in expectation by stating their true belief; a rule that pays for shading toward a favoured answer is not proper. Sempere and Lawsen {cite:r5} showed that a mean {g:brier}Brier score{/g} gives a forecaster a reason to skip. The Brier score, from weather forecasting, is the squared difference between the stated probabilities and what happened, so lower is better; it scores each answer given and says nothing about questions left unanswered: a forecaster whose average Brier score is {m:b^2} should not forecast any question whose true probability lies between {m:b} and {m:1 - b}, even when they know it exactly. Skipping and scoring are therefore tangled before any data is read.

Machine learning has a matching problem under the name {g:selective-prediction}selective prediction{/g}. A classifier with a reject option keeps the inputs it is most confident on and declines the rest; the term covers that choice of what to answer and leaves out how the kept answers are made. Its quality is drawn as a {g:risk-coverage}risk-coverage curve{/g}, the error on kept inputs against the share kept {cite:r6}. Here risk is the mean Brier score of kept forecasts and coverage the share kept, so the curve says nothing about the forecasts withheld. We use the same curve to score abstain filters for human forecasts.

The third question concerns the hedge. An earlier round of this study found that a forecast a person rates as expertise 1 is worse than the same person's higher-rated forecasts and sits nearer 50 percent. {g:extremising}Extremising{/g}, the transformation Baron, Mellers and colleagues studied for aggregated forecasts {cite:r4}, pushes a probability away from 50 percent by scaling its log-odds by a fixed factor, and a factor below 1 pulls it inward instead; it changes no forecast's direction. It can test whether that pull toward 50 percent is too large, too small or the right size.

The study was built to inform one design choice: how the abstain filter in Flywheel, our accountability software, should rank a source's answers. Should it credit a source for abstaining, and does it need the source's self-rating beside the stated probability?

sections.title: Preregistration and design
paragraphs: This is the second round of the study. The {g:preregistration}preregistration{/g}, a practice from clinical trials and psychology in which a dated plan is fixed before results are seen, was written on 29 October 2026 after the first round's results and before any second-round statistic was computed on the real data, and it was hash-locked at 14:59:09 UTC that day. A plan revised after a look at second-round outcomes would not have counted as one. It lists what had been seen before it was written: the first round's results and structural counts of conditions, first forecasts and repeat forecasters taken from the survey files with no outcome joined.

The second-round code was checked first on synthetic files shaped like the GJP data, with {g:planted-check}planted effects{/g} that the code recovered. That is a planted check: data built so the right answer is known, run through the same analysis before the real data, to show the analysis can find an effect when it is there, which no check on real data can show. That check showed that matching on the number of questions answered removes most of the variation in skip rate, because skip rate is one minus answered over available. Matching on forecast count therefore stayed the primary design, as in the first round. This is recorded in the preregistration.

The file names ten {g:verdict}verdicts{/g} in four parts, each with rules that must all hold, seven shuffle {g:control}controls{/g} with their draw counts, a prior probability for each verdict, and a decision mapping from outcomes to the filter design. A verdict, in our usage, is the pass or fail of one such rule set read off by code, never a reading written after the numbers were seen. A control is a copy of the data with one link broken, by shuffling, and scored with the same code as the real data; a comparison with another dataset or a published number is not a control. Appendix A gives every verdict and its rule. Nothing was added after the run.

sections.title: Data and provenance
paragraphs: The data are the Good Judgment Project survey forecasts for years 1 to 4 and the question file, published by Mellers and colleagues on the Harvard Dataverse (doi:10.7910/DVN/BPCDH5) under {g:cc0}CC0 1.0{/g} {cite:r1}. CC0 is the Creative Commons public domain dedication: anyone may reuse the data for any purpose without permission, and citation is a scholarly courtesy rather than a licence term. The person-level test file and the {g:prediction-market}prediction-market{/g} files in the same release were not used; in a prediction market people trade contracts that pay on an outcome and the price is read as a probability, which is a different instrument from the survey forecasts used here. The {g:sha-256}SHA-256{/g} of each of the five input files was recorded before the run and matched after it. SHA-256 is a cryptographic hash, a 64-character fingerprint that changes if any byte of a file changes; it shows the files were not altered and keeps nothing secret.

The survey files hold 3,143,460 rows, one per answer option. Dropping 43,944 withdrawal rows left 1,234,940 forecasts. Of the 617 questions, 498 closed with an outcome and 119 were {g:voided-question}voided{/g}. A voided question is one the tournament cancelled without scoring, a tournament term with no bearing on the verdict sense of void. We dropped 157,189 forecasts on voided or unresolved questions, 13,381 dated after the question closed and 15 whose probabilities could not be repaired. That leaves 1,064,355 scored forecasts from 9,914 people, of which 414,570 are a person's first forecast on a question in a year.

Self-rated expertise, 1 to 5 on each forecast, exists in years 1 to 3 only; all 619,380 year 4 forecasts lack it. The abstain-filter sample is therefore every binary scored forecast in years 1 to 3 with a rating: 410,451 forecasts. Experimental conditions 1 and 2 are individuals, 4 teams and 5 {g:superteam}superteams{/g}. A superteam, in the project's design, is a team made up of forecasters drawn from the top performers of the previous year; ordinary teams were formed without that selection. The prediction-market condition is not in the survey files.

The data hold no record of a declined question. A {g:skip}skip{/g} is inferred: a closed question that was open during a forecaster's active window in a year and that they never answered. The word is ours for that inferred absence, and it excludes questions that closed before or opened after the forecaster's active window. Only aggregates and distributions are reported here. No score for any named person was stored.

sections.title: Methods
paragraphs: ## Scoring
Each forecast is scored with the Brier score in the GJP form, summed over the answer options, so that it runs from 0 to 2:
$$ B = \sum_{k} (p_k - o_k)^2 {eq:brier}

where {m:p_k} is the stated probability of option {m:k} and {m:o_k} is 1 if that option occurred and 0 otherwise. The {g:relative-brier}relative score{/g} of forecaster {m:i} on first forecasts is the mean, over the {m:n_i} questions they answered, of their first-forecast Brier score minus the median first-forecast Brier score on that question. It is our measure of skill against the crowd on the same question, and it leaves out how hard the question was, which the median absorbs:
$$ S_i = \frac{1}{n_i} \sum_{q} (B_{iq} - m_q) {eq:rel}

The time-matched version {m:S_{i,t}} takes the median {m:m_q} only over first forecasts made in the same tenth of the question's open period, drops cells with fewer than 5 first forecasts, and needs 5 or more valid questions per {g:forecaster-year}forecaster-year{/g}, our unit of analysis: one person's forecasts within one tournament year, so a person active in three years counts three times and no two people are pooled. Lower {m:S} is better, so the tests correlate skip rate with {m:-S}.
## Skip rate and the matched correlation
A forecaster-year is eligible with at least 10 available questions and 5 answered. Its skip rate is
$$ s_i = 1 - \frac{n_{ans}}{n_{av}} {eq:skip}

where {m:n_{ans}} is the number of available questions answered and {m:n_{av}} the number available. Busy forecasters answer more, so the correlation is taken inside {g:stratum}strata{/g} {m:h} of year and twentieth of forecast count, each with 10 or more forecaster-years, and averaged with weights {m:w_h} equal to stratum size. A stratum, a term from survey statistics, is a group of units alike on the matched variables, so comparisons inside it cannot be driven by those variables; it does nothing about variables left unmatched:
$$ \rho_M = \frac{\sum_h w_h \rho_h}{\sum_h w_h} {eq:rhom}

where {m:\rho_h} is the {g:spearman}Spearman correlation{/g} of {m:s_i} with {m:-S_i} inside stratum {m:h}. Spearman's rho, from rank statistics, is the correlation of the ranks of two quantities, so it reads any steady rise or fall and ignores the shape of the relation and the size of outliers. {g:interval-95}Intervals{/g} come from 1,000 {g:bootstrap}bootstrap{/g} draws within strata. Each 95 percent interval is the range holding the middle 95 percent of the draws, and it is no statement that the true value lies inside with 95 percent probability. The bootstrap, a resampling method from statistics, recomputes the number on data resampled with replacement and assumes no textbook distribution.

The within-person test takes pairs of consecutive years in which a person kept the same majority condition. Inside each year pair it computes the Spearman correlation of the change in skip rate with the change in time-matched score, and averages over year pairs weighted by pair count. Changing condition between years would change the platform and the questions, so mixed pairs are left out of the primary test.
## The size of the hedge
For a stated probability {m:p} the extremised probability is
$$ p' = \frac{p^a}{p^a + (1 - p)^a} {eq:ext}

so the {g:log-odds}log-odds{/g} are multiplied by {m:a}. The log-odds of a probability {m:p}, a term from statistics, is {m:\ln(p / (1 - p))}, which is 0 at 50 percent and grows without bound toward certainty; it is a rescaling of the probability and adds no information to it. A value {m:a} above 1 means forecasts were too hedged, below 1 too extreme, and 1 right-sized. The factor is fitted by minimum Brier score on a grid from 0.30 to 4.00 in steps of 0.01. Questions were split once at random into two halves; the {g:held-out}held-out gain{/g} is the Brier score at {m:a = 1} minus the Brier score at the {m:a} fitted on the other half, summed over both halves and taken per forecast. Held-out, in machine-learning usage, means scored on data the fit never saw, which excludes the in-sample improvement any fitted factor gives. The primary contrast uses the first round's within-person sample: forecaster-years with at least 5 forecasts at expertise 1 and 5 at expertise 2 to 5. Intervals come from 1,000 bootstrap draws over questions.
## Abstain filters

A filter ranks forecasts by predicted Brier score and keeps the best-ranked share {m:c}, the coverage. Its risk {m:R(c)} is the mean raw Brier score of the kept forecasts. Each predictor is an {g:out-of-fold}out-of-fold{/g} cell mean, computed for each forecast from the other folds only, so no forecast helps predict itself: the self-rating filter uses the five expertise levels, the probability filter ten bins of distance from 0.5 in steps of 0.05, and the combined filter their 50 crossed cells, falling back to the probability bin where a cell has fewer than 30 training forecasts. Ties are broken by one fixed random key. The summary is the {g:aurc}area under the risk-coverage curve{/g}, taken as the mean risk over 19 coverages. The area is a selective-prediction summary of a whole filter in one number, lower being better, and it excludes coverages below 10 percent:
$$ A = \frac{1}{19} \sum_{j} R(c_j) {eq:aurc}
with {m:j} running from 1 to 19 and {m:c_j = 0.05 (j + 1)}, so coverage runs from 0.10 to 1.00. Lower is better. A random filter keeps the overall mean at every coverage.
## Controls and p values

Every shuffle control is scored with the same code as the real data. The {g:p-value-draws}p value{/g} of a comparison, a p value from draws as in permutation statistics, assumes no textbook distribution and counts the control draws at or above the real value, with one added to the numerator and the denominator:
$$ p = \frac{k + 1}{n + 1} {eq:p}
where {m:k} is the number of draws at or above the real value and {m:n} the number of draws. At 1,000 draws the smallest possible value is 0.001.

sections.title: Controls and planted checks
paragraphs: Seven controls were fixed in the preregistration. Each breaks one link and keeps the rest of the data. The scores a control gives over its draws form a null distribution, whose 95th percentile is the bar a real score must clear; it is drawn from these data, never assumed from theory.
- Skip rate shuffled within year and forecast-count strata, the {g:null-distribution}null{/g} for the first-forecast correlation (1,000 draws), and the same on the time-matched table (1,000).
- Change in skip rate shuffled within year pair, the null for the within-person test (1,000).
- The expertise-1 label shuffled within forecaster-year with the question halves fixed, the null for the difference in extremising gain (300).

- Expertise shuffled within forecaster-year with all predictors refitted, the null for the gain from adding the rating to the probability filter (300). This asks whether the rating carries information about one forecast or only about who is rating.
- The team label shuffled across forecaster-years within year, the null for the team-against-individual differences in skip effect and in filter gain (300 each).

The random filter is the known floor: Brier 0.277 at every coverage. Before the real data were read, the code recovered planted effects in synthetic files of the same shape: skippers sharper on first forecasts, a within-person change, and over-hedged expertise-1 forecasts. The first round also carried a {g:positive-control}positive control{/g} that passed, a test of an effect already known to be there, which the instrument must detect for its other readings to be trusted: one point of self-rated expertise improved relative Brier by 0.0226 (0.0185 to 0.0270) within forecaster-years, against a shuffle 95th percentile of 0.0015. Every control in this round had enough spread to be usable.

sections.title: Results
paragraphs: ## Abstain filters

Figure {ref:fig:rc} draws the three risk-coverage curves and Table {ref:tab:filters} gives their areas. {c1}A filter on the stated probability scored 0.171, a filter on the self-rating 0.259, and random order 0.277.{/c1} The probability filter gains 0.107 (0.097 to 0.115) over random, and the self-rating filter 0.018 (0.009 to 0.027), about a sixth as much.

![fig:rc width=0.88 alt=Three risk-coverage curves; the self-rating curve stays near the random line while the probability and combined curves fall steeply](fig-risk-coverage.png) Mean Brier score of kept forecasts against coverage for the three filters, on 410,451 binary forecasts from years 1 to 3. Squares mark two rules a person could apply by hand: withhold every expertise-1 forecast (coverage 0.78) and withhold expertise 1 and 2 (coverage 0.48), each against the probability filter at the same coverage. Drawn from the run's result file.

::table tab:filters cols=0.4,0.18,0.42 Area under the risk-coverage curve (raw Brier, 0 to 2 scale; lower is better). Intervals are 95 percent bootstraps over questions.
Filter ¦ Area ¦ Gain and interval
Random order ¦ 0.277 ¦ reference
Self-rated expertise ¦ 0.259 ¦ 0.018 over random (0.009 to 0.027)
Stated probability ¦ 0.171 ¦ 0.107 over random (0.097 to 0.115)
Both together ¦ 0.168 ¦ 0.0026 over probability (0.0007 to 0.0046)
Both, rating shuffled within forecaster-year ¦ not reported ¦ 0.0024 over probability on average; 95th percentile 0.0030; p 0.31
::end

{c2}Adding the self-rating to the probability gained 0.0026 (95 percent interval 0.0007 to 0.0046), under the preregistered bar of 0.005, and a rating shuffled within each forecaster-year gained 0.0024 on average.{/c2} The interval excludes zero, so the combined filter is better than the probability alone by a small amount. The shuffle buys nearly all of it: the small edge comes from who rates themselves high on average. The rating given to one forecast adds nothing past that. The combined filter leads by 0.007 to 0.011 in Brier score up to coverage 0.25, and by 0.004 or less above that. Relative Brier gives the same order: areas 0.124 for self-rating, 0.063 for probability, 0.061 for both and 0.134 for random.

The by-hand rules lose to the probability filter at the same coverage. Withholding every expertise-1 forecast keeps 78 percent of forecasts at Brier 0.267; the probability filter at that coverage reaches 0.214 and the combined filter 0.214. Withholding expertise 1 and 2 keeps 48 percent at 0.259, against 0.141 for the probability filter and 0.142 combined.
## Skipping and first forecasts

Figure {ref:fig:skip} and Table {ref:tab:skip} give the skip correlations. Across the 9,204 eligible forecaster-years (1,781; 1,114; 1,360 and 4,949 in years 1 to 4), the median skip rate was 0.59. {c3}On first forecasts only, skip rate correlated with better relative Brier score at rho +0.286 (+0.264 to +0.303) across 9,204 forecaster-years, and +0.195 (+0.174 to +0.212) when timing was matched as well.{/c3} The first round's statistic on all forecasts, updates included, recomputed on the same table, was +0.351, so removing every update keeps about 80 percent of it.

![fig:skip width=0.86 alt=Diamonds with interval bars for five skip correlations; four sit well right of zero and the same-person estimate straddles zero](fig-skip.png) Matched Spearman correlations of skip rate with better relative Brier score, with 95 percent intervals (bars) and the shuffle control's 95th percentile (grey ticks) where the preregistration set one. Drawn from the run's result file.

Skippers enter questions later. Inside strata, skip rate correlates +0.41 with the mean timing of a person's first forecasts, and matching on timing removes about a third of the first-forecast effect. Inside the same strata skip rate also correlates +0.452 with updates per answered question, and updates per question correlate +0.178 with better first-forecast score: people who update a lot also make better first forecasts.

{c4}Within the same person across consecutive years the correlation was +0.041 (-0.007 to +0.095) over 1,578 pairs, so no within-person benefit of skipping was shown.{/c4} The pairs split 501, 469 and 608 across years 1 to 2, 2 to 3 and 3 to 4. The estimate sits just under the shuffle's 95th percentile of +0.041 (p 0.055). The test had room to see an effect of cross-sectional size: {g:test-retest}test-retest correlation{/g}, the psychometric term for how well one person's value in one year predicts the same person's value the next, is 0.62 for skip rate and 0.46 for score, skip rate changed by a standard deviation of 0.25 between years, and the upper bound of +0.095 is under half the time-matched cross-section. All 1,962 pairs, mixed conditions included, give +0.031 (-0.013 to +0.075).

::table tab:skip cols=0.4,0.13,0.21,0.13,0.13 Skip rate against better relative Brier score. Shuffle values are the control's 95th percentile; p from eq. {ref:eq:p}.
Test ¦ rho ¦ 95 percent interval ¦ Shuffle ¦ p
First forecasts, 9,204 forecaster-years ¦ +0.286 ¦ +0.264 to +0.303 ¦ +0.018 ¦ 0.001
First forecasts, timing matched ¦ +0.195 ¦ +0.174 to +0.212 ¦ +0.018 ¦ 0.001
Same person, 1,578 pairs ¦ +0.041 ¦ -0.007 to +0.095 ¦ +0.041 ¦ 0.055
Teams, timing matched, 3,248 ¦ +0.162 ¦ +0.123 to +0.196 ¦ none ¦ none
Individuals, timing matched, 5,956 ¦ +0.148 ¦ +0.119 to +0.172 ¦ none ¦ none
::end

Teams skip more than individuals (median skip rate 0.63 against 0.57), but the skip effect did not differ detectably: the gap of 0.013 sits under the label-shuffle 95th percentile of 0.043. Superteams removed, condition 4 alone gives +0.154. The gain from adding the self-rating to the filter was 0.0033 in teams and 0.0008 for individuals, a gap of 0.0025 against a shuffle 95th percentile of 0.0030 (p 0.11).
## The size of the hedge

In the within-person sample (1,826 forecaster-years; 77,572 forecasts rated 1 and 165,914 rated 2 to 5), {c5}forecasts rated expertise 1 are pulled toward 50 percent by about the right amount: the best extremising factor was 0.92 (0.79 to 1.06).{/c5} The held-out gain from extremising them was +0.0002 (-0.0010 to +0.0016). Forecasts rated 2 to 5 gave 0.93 (0.81 to 1.04), a difference of -0.01 (-0.09 to +0.08). Extremising helped neither group: the gain for low-rated forecasts minus the gain for high-rated ones was -0.0001 (-0.0009 to +0.0008). Table {ref:tab:cal} shows the folded calibration behind these numbers.

::table tab:cal cols=0.16,0.14,0.14,0.14,0.14,0.14,0.14 Folded calibration in the within-person sample: the stated probability on the side the forecast leans to, against how often that side happened.
Stated ¦ Rated 1, n ¦ Stated ¦ Hit rate ¦ Rated 2 to 5, n ¦ Stated ¦ Hit rate
0.5 to 0.6 ¦ 4,664 ¦ 0.546 ¦ 0.553 ¦ 6,968 ¦ 0.549 ¦ 0.537
0.6 to 0.7 ¦ 12,332 ¦ 0.624 ¦ 0.618 ¦ 22,097 ¦ 0.626 ¦ 0.602
0.7 to 0.8 ¦ 12,558 ¦ 0.727 ¦ 0.710 ¦ 25,197 ¦ 0.728 ¦ 0.713
0.8 to 0.9 ¦ 13,360 ¦ 0.826 ¦ 0.821 ¦ 29,612 ¦ 0.827 ¦ 0.822
0.9 to 1.0 ¦ 29,954 ¦ 0.957 ¦ 0.911 ¦ 78,706 ¦ 0.959 ¦ 0.930
::end

Folded {g:ece}expected calibration error{/g} was 0.024 for low-rated and 0.021 for high-rated forecasts; 4,704 low-rated and 3,334 high-rated forecasts sat at exactly 0.5. Expected calibration error, a forecasting and machine-learning measure, is the gap between stated probability and hit rate averaged over the bins of Table {ref:tab:cal}, weighted by bin size; it measures whether forecasts mean what they say and is silent on how informative they are. Across all binary forecasts in years 1 to 3, with people pooled, Figure {ref:fig:ext} gives the factor by level. Only the top of the scale misses: forecasts rated 4 or 5 were over-extreme, with a factor of 0.82 (0.68 to 0.96), and at stated probabilities from 0.6 to 0.9 their hit rate ran 0.04 to 0.06 under what they stated.

![fig:ext width=0.8 alt=Best extremising factor with intervals for four expertise levels; three intervals cross 1 and the top level sits below it](fig-extremise.png) Best extremising factor {m:a} by self-rated expertise, all binary forecasts in years 1 to 3 with people pooled, with 95 percent intervals over questions. A factor of 1 means right-sized; below 1 means too extreme. Drawn from the run's result file.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: The filter result has a plain mechanism. A forecast near 0 or 1 scores well when it is right, and calibrated forecasters are right about as often as they say. Ranking by stated probability therefore keeps the forecasts that will score best, and part of the gain is arithmetic: the filter rewards confidence by construction. This is the same arithmetic Sempere and Lawsen {cite:r5} point to when they show that a mean Brier score pays a forecaster to skip questions in the middle of the probability range. For a filter that only needs to lower the error of what it emits, the arithmetic is the point. For a claim that confident forecasters know more, it is not evidence.

The self-rating adds little because the stated probability already carries it. The first round read "worse and nearer 0.5" as the rating carrying information past the probability. The hedge results settle that point. Expertise-1 forecasts are pulled toward 50 percent by the amount their information warrants, and their worse Brier score is what a calibrated, less informed forecast scores. Once a filter sees the probability, the per-forecast rating adds nothing a within-person shuffle does not also add. The one place the rating says something the probability does not is at the top: forecasters who rate themselves 4 or 5 are over-extreme, so a top rating works as a warning sign for overconfidence.

On skipping, the data separate a trait from an act. People who habitually answer selectively score better on their first forecasts, before any update, at matched timing, in teams and individuals alike. A person who skips more this year than last does not clearly gain from it. Skip rate works as a marker of a careful forecaster; the data do not show that abstaining improves an answer. Merkle and colleagues {cite:r3} asked whether good and poor forecasters select questions differently in the same tournament. An earlier search note of ours recorded that they found good forecasters selecting more questions, a sign that runs against ours before matching. We read their abstract only, so we cannot confirm the sign or say whether our forecast-count strata, which compare people of equal activity, account for the difference.

For the filter design, the decision mapping fixed in advance gives a direct reading. The filter ranks by stated probability. It does not take the self-rating as an add-on; a high self-rating is at most a flag to soften a forecast. A habit of abstaining can raise the weight given to a source, but abstention is not credited as something that improves an answer. One setting serves teams and individuals. All of this is human data. For model sources it sets the design to test, not the setting: a model's stated probabilities need their own check against outcomes.

sections.title: Limitations
paragraphs: - Skips are inferred. A question counted as skipped may have been unseen, or outside the forecaster's condition; "available" is any closed question open during their active window.
- Nothing here is causal. People chose their ratings, their questions and when to forecast.

- The within-person interval reaches +0.095, which leaves room for a small benefit of skipping. Between years the platform, the question mix and the training also changed; same-condition pairs only reduce this.
- Updating, timing and selection remain tangled in the cross-section: skip rate correlates +0.452 with updates per question inside strata.
- A probability filter lowers Brier partly by arithmetic, as the discussion sets out.
- The filters were simulated after the fact on forecasts people chose to make with no filter in place. A live filter would change behaviour.
- Year 4 has no self-ratings, prediction-market trades were not used, and nothing here speaks for language models.
- Merkle and colleagues studied question selection in the same tournament and may disagree on the sign; we read only their abstract.
- Scoring was done by our own code and was not blind.

claims.text: A filter on the stated probability scored 0.171, a filter on the self-rating 0.259, and random order 0.277.

Adding the self-rating to the probability gained 0.0026 (95 percent interval 0.0007 to 0.0046), under the preregistered bar of 0.005, and a rating shuffled within each forecaster-year gained 0.0024 on average.

On first forecasts only, skip rate correlated with better relative Brier score at rho +0.286 (+0.264 to +0.303) across 9,204 forecaster-years, and +0.195 (+0.174 to +0.212) when timing was matched as well.
Within the same person across consecutive years the correlation was +0.041 (-0.007 to +0.095) over 1,578 pairs, so no within-person benefit of skipping was shown.
Forecasts rated expertise 1 are pulled toward 50 percent by about the right amount: the best extremising factor was 0.92 (0.79 to 1.06).

steps: Data: download the GJP survey forecasts (years 1 to 4) and the question file from the Harvard Dataverse, doi:10.7910/DVN/BPCDH5.
Drop withdrawals, forecasts on voided or unresolved questions, forecasts dated after close and unrepairable probabilities. Score each forecast with eq. {ref:eq:brier}.

For each forecaster-year with at least 10 available and 5 answered questions, compute the skip rate (eq. {ref:eq:skip}) and the first-forecast relative score (eq. {ref:eq:rel}), plain and time-matched. Take the matched correlation (eq. {ref:eq:rhom}) inside year and forecast-count strata, and the within-person version on same-condition consecutive-year pairs.
Fit the extremising factor (eq. {ref:eq:ext}) by grid search with a random split of questions into halves.

Rank binary forecasts from years 1 to 3 by out-of-fold predicted Brier from self-rating, probability bin and both, and take the area (eq. {ref:eq:aurc}). Shuffle the rating within forecaster-year and refit as the control.
